As waterfalls a thousand [music] meters tall, a lake glows a milky impossible turquoise beneath [music] bare brown mountains. A wild beach curves away for miles without one footprint on it. [music] This is New Zealand. Two long green islands and a scatter of small ones. a drift in the far southwest [music] Pacific, home to 5.3 million people, living about as far from the rest of the world as it is possible to live. [music] Here is the strange part. This was the last great landmass human [music] beings ever found. When the first Maui canoes touched these beaches around the year 1300, the pyramids of Egypt were [music] already 3 and a half thousand years old. It is a country with no native land mammals at all, where birds forgot how to fly because nothing ever hunted them. And its sheep once outnumbered [music] its people 22 to1. [music] Today we cross New Zealand from a barefoot morning in a small town to a hut that lies 2 days [music] walk from the nearest road chasing one question. What kind of life do people build at the very end of [music] the earth? Stay with us to the very end. You will meet the most [music] famous sheep this planet has ever known and the most isolated family in the country. [music] Morning [music] in a New Zealand town starts with a detail that stops every newcomer midstep. People are shopping barefoot in the supermarket, at the post office, [music] on the school run, bare feet on clean lenolium in a wealthy modern country and absolutely nobody looks [music] twice. It is not poverty and it is not protest. It is simply comfort worn openly. The national attitude you will find walks the same way. The day's first ritual is [music] coffee taken seriously. The flat white espresso under a thin blanket of velvet milk is the local heartbeat. And New Zealand and Australia have argued for decades about which of them invented it. The feud is conducted entirely with smiles and no one intends to settle it. What matters is that in towns of a few hundred people at the edge of the map, the coffee is often better than in the capitals of Europe. [music] Out past the towns, the school bus works [music] the gravel roads, collecting children from farm gates an hour apart. And on those same roads, you meet the country's true traffic jam. A river of sheep filling the road from [music] fence to fence flows around your stopped car like water around a stone. A dog trots the edges and the farmer raises one finger from the wheel. The standard rural salute. You do not honk. You wait and you wave back. Weekends drift [music] toward the Bach. The little family holiday house deliberately plain, furnished with mismatched chairs, and someone's retired teapot. Jandles by the door, fishing rods in the rafters, fish and chips eaten straight from the paper on the sand. The unofficial [music] national motto covers all of it. She'll be right. Meaning, it will work out. It usually does. And when it does not [music] work out, a kiwi reaches for number eight wire. That is the standard gauge of fencing wire. And it has become the country's shorthand for its own character. The belief runs deep with a length of wire and some thought. A person at the end of the world can fix nearly anything. Remember that confidence. This whole country runs on it. And it began as so much here began with sheep. [music] Run the numbers and New Zealand is still at heart a nation of sheep. 23.6 million of them against 5.3 million people. Between 4 and five sheep for every single [music] citizen. And that is the modest era. Back in 1982, [music] the flock stood at over 20 sheep per person. And wool built this country the way oil built others. The roads, [music] the towns, the fine stone houses of the south. The high country is [music] where that world survives. Sheep stations in the southern mountains stretch across areas the size of small nations worked by musterers [music] on horseback and quadbikes and by dogs worth their weight in wages. [music] Shearing gangs still move from shed to shed in season and a good shearer dripping sweat can strip a sheep in under a minute. The sheep as a rule [music] cooperate. One of them famously did not. [music] His name was Shrek. He belonged to Bendigo Station, a vast marino run in central Otago owned by a farmer named John Perium. And one year at Muster, [music] Shrek simply failed to show up, nor the next year, nor the year after that. For 6 years, the weather hid in rock caves above [music] the station, dodging every roundup, growing woollier and woollier. Then, in 2004, [music] a muster finally cornered a creature so enormous and shapeless that at first he could not tell what animal it was. The fleece weighed 27 kg. Enough wool, the shearers calculated, to make suits for 20 [music] grown men. Shrek was shown live on national television while the country watched. And then things turned [music] properly strange. The sheep toured children's hospitals. He raised money for charity. He was walked into parliament to meet [music] the prime minister, Helen Clark. and posed for the cameras like a professional. [music] When Shrek died in 2011 at nearly 17, the news led national bulletins and grown farmers spoke of him with soft voices. Foreigners found the whole affair baffling. New Zealanders [music] did not even try to explain. A small country at the bottom of the world [music] had seen itself in one stubborn, shaggy escape artist. And besides, people here have always respected anyone [music] who takes to the hills on their own terms, including, as we are about to see, the first people of all. [music] Every other great landmass met human beings tens of thousands of years [music] ago. This one waited while empires rose and crumbled [music] elsewhere. These two islands stayed empty of people. Forests full of bird song. beaches printed only by gulls for thousands of years after the [music] pyramids, after Rome, after almost everything. The last major land on Earth without a human footprint. [music] [music] Then around 7 and 1/2 centuries ago, the ocean delivered its greatest navigators. Maui ancestors came from tropical east Polynesia in doublehauled sailing [music] canoes called waka crossing thousands of kilometers of open Pacific with no instruments reading stars swells and the flight lines of birds. Somewhere around the year 1300, give or take a [music] generation, those canoes ran ashore here. It was the final chapter of humanity's longest journey. [music] And the navigators named the new world for what they saw [music] from the sea. Aaroa, often translated as the land of the long white cloud. In this young country, Maui built an old and intricate world. Fortified hillside villages, genealogies recited like scripture, carving and [music] weaving that turned ancestry into art. Then in 1840 at a place called Wangi [music] in the Bay of Islands, Mauri chiefs and the British crown signed the treaty that founded modern New Zealand. Its [music] promises have been argued over ever since, honored, broken, and slowly repaired. But the date [music] remains the country's birth and why Tangi its birthplace. [music] Perhaps because everything here was [music] newly built, this country kept trying things nobody else dared. In 1893, New Zealand became the first nation on Earth where women [music] could vote, decades ahead of Britain or the United States after a campaigner [music] named Kate Shepard hauled petitions the length of the [music] country. Her face now looks out from the $10 note, a quiet daily reminder of the day the world's [music] youngest country led it. So hold both truths at once. This is the last land [music] humans ever found. And it has spent its short human history running ahead of everyone. New arrivals, old wisdom, first in the world laws, all of it stacked onto islands. Most maps [music] push into a corner. And the culture that arrived in those first canoes is not behind glass in a museum. It still [music] stands at the door waiting to welcome you properly. To be welcomed onto a marai, the carved meeting ground at the heart of every Maui community, is to pass through a ceremony older than the country's name. It is called a powheri. A challenge is [music] laid down and answered. A woman's voice rises in a long keening [music] call. Speeches flow in Maui. Songs answer the speeches and visitors walk forward slowly. Guests until the ritual makes [music] them something more. It ends with the hongji. Two people press noses and foreheads together once gently. And with that touch, hosts and strangers share the same breath. The breath [music] of life. as elders explain it, the one the gods breathed into the first woman. After the hongi, tradition holds, you are no longer a visitor. You share the breath of the house, [music] and a place is set for you at the table. And what a table. For a feast, the cooking is done by the land itself in an earth oven called a hangy. A pit is dug at dawn. Stones are heated in a fire until they glow. Then laid in the bottom and down go baskets of lamb, pork, chicken, potatoes, pumpkin, and kumar, the maui sweet potato. The whole thing is wrapped, [music] buried, and left. Hours later, the earth is opened like a lid. Steam rolls out and the food lifts free, tasting [music] of smoke, soil, and patience. [music] The world knows one Maui tradition above all, the haka. The thundering posture [music] dance the All Blacks perform before rugby matches. All slapped chests [music] and shaking ground. What the world often misses is that the haker was never only a war dance and never only for stadiums. New Zealanders hucker at weddings, at graduations, at [music] funerals until the coffin has gone at airport arrival gates, welcoming someone home while strangers [music] stop and film through tears. Because that is what it is in [music] the end. Emotion with nowhere else to put itself. A country often teased for being quiet and [music] practical keeps at its center a ceremony where grown men weep openly and nobody looks away. The first arrivals gave this land its loudest heartbeat. Its strangest inhabitants, though, had been here long before, and they have feathers. Now for the fact that shaped everything on these islands when they broke away from the ancient superc continent. New Zealand's islands sailed off without land mammals. None ever except a few small bats. No deer, no foxes, no cats, no rats. For millions of years, nothing here hunted on the ground. So the birds with no reason to flee gradually gave up the one thing that makes a bird a bird. They stopped flying. The most famous of them is the kiwi. Round, flightless, nocturnal, whiskered like a cat with nostrils at the tip of its long beak. the only bird on Earth built that way. It sniffs out worms in the dark like a small feathered badger and it lays one of the largest eggs for its body size in the entire bird world. New Zealanders adopted it so completely that they named themselves after it. This may be the only nation on the planet nicknamed for a bird that cannot fly [music] and only comes out at night. At the other end of the temperament scale lives the Kia, the world's only alpine parrot. Olive green, brilliant, and criminally bored. key open zippers, raid bins, and dismantle parked cars in ski field lots, peeling rubber seals off windcreens with surgical patients while their owners watch helplessly [music] from the cafe. Scientists rank them among the most intelligent birds alive. Locals rank them somewhere between national [music] treasure and organized crime. Stranger [music] still is the touatara, a spiny reptile that looks like a lizard but is not one. Its family line is older than the dinosaurs. It can live well past 100 and on the top of its skull, it carries a third eye complete with a lens hidden under scales. And in the limestone caves of Witomo, a native glowworm [music] turns whole ceilings into blue green constellations. An underground night sky thousands of visitors drift beneath in silent boats. When rats, stos, and psums finally [music] did arrive on ships, they tore through birds that had never learned fear. So New Zealanders went to war for their strange neighbors. They fenced off [music] entire valleys, cleared island sanctuaries like Ulva of every predator, and set [music] a national goal that sounds like science fiction. A whole country predator free. Ask the rangers who trap the hills in the rain why they bother, and the answer is usually simple. Nowhere else has these creatures. Somebody has to be their army. Cross the center of the North Island and the [music] ground starts talking. In the city of Rotarooa, steam rises casually from storm drains, from [music] cracks in the pavement, from the corners of ordinary backyards. Mudpools mutter and pop behind motel car parks. The air carries a faint sulfur tang that residents stop smelling within a week, and visitors mention within a minute. This is what living on the Pacific Ring of Fire looks like when a city simply refuses [music] to be impressed by it. refuses and profits. For more than a century, locals here have plumbed the planet's heat straight into daily life. Homes and pools warm themselves on [music] geothermal water. In the Maui village of Wakarea, families still cook the way their ancestors did. Corn and puddings lowered into boiling mineral [music] pools. Meals steamed in wooden boxes set over natural vents in the earth. Dinner cooked by the inside of the planet on a Tuesday. [music] The volcanoes themselves stand [music] an hour south in Tongerro National Park, the country's oldest. It was born in 1887 when, as the story is told, [music] a great Maui chief gifted the sacred peaks to the nation so they could never be carved up and sold. The world took note twice over. Tongerro is listed as a dual world heritage site, honored once for its volcanic landscape and once for what that landscape means to Maui. Walk the famous Alpine [music] Crossing and the planet shows off shamelessly steaming red craters, black lava fields, and a string of small lakes so mineral green they look poured from a paint tin. In winter, skiers [music] carve down the slopes of Ruapahoo, an active volcano wearing a ski resort. Because in New Zealand, even the hazards are expected to earn their keep as scenery. [music] There is a national temperament visible in all this steam. The ground here has never pretended to be finished, and neither have the people on it. You build anyway, plant anyway, ski the volcano anyway, and [music] keep the kettle warm on whatever the earth is doing that day. Farther south, the drama goes quiet [music] and turns to sheer ridiculous beauty. The kind that made this country a screen legend. [music] Milford [music] Sound sits so deep in the southwest corner that the road in took nearly a century to [music] build and the first sight of it has been ending arguments ever since. Sheer [music] cliffs rise a mile from Blackwater and Miter Peak stands [music] in the fjord like a cathedral that grew there. Sailors named it a sound and the name stuck. It is actually a fjord gouged [music] out by glaciers. one mislabel this country has happily never corrected. [music] The trick of Milford is that bad weather improves it. It is one of [music] the wetest inhabited places on Earth. And when the rain comes down, the cliffs [music] sprout waterfalls by the hund ribbons of white unspooling from the clouds themselves. [music] Most of them nameless, many gone by morning. Visitors who get rained on feel cheated for an hour, then realize they have seen the better show. [music] [music] In land rises Araki, Mount Cook, the country's rooftop at 3,700 [music] m. In the Maui telling, Araki was a boy in a sky canoe [music] that ran a ground. He and his brothers climbed onto the hull and froze into the southern Alps. The mountain is an ancestor first and a [music] summit second, which is why by agreement climbers today stop just short of treading the very highest point of his head. [music] [music] Below Araki spreads a basin that looks painted. Lake Takapo glows that improbable milky turquoise [music] rock ground to flower by glacias hanging in the meltwater and catching the light. On its shore stands a tiny stone [music] church with a window that frames the lake instead of an altar painting. And overhead, night brings the region's [music] second lake of stars. The skies here are protected as one of the world's great dark sky [music] reserves. So black that the Milky Way casts the faintest of [music] shadows. [music] And down on the wild west coast, two glaciers, Fox [music] and France Joseph, pour off the Alps to end almost at sea level. White ice hanging above green rainforest minutes from the beach. Almost nowhere else on Earth do those [music] worlds touch. New Zealanders, true to form, treat all of it as the daily backdrop. There are school buses down here that commute without comment past a fjord. [music] Follow the coast [music] to the very bottom of the South Island and you reach the Catlands. The corner the crowds [music] forget. Sea lions haul out and doze on empty beaches like dropped luggage. Yellow-eyed penguins, among the rarest on Earth, waddle up through the dunes at dusk. There is a petrified forest in the [music] tide zone, a lighthouse on a windbent point, and a small sign at slope point giving the distance [music] to the equator and to the south pole. The pole is closer than most visitors expect. [music] Out here, the town's thin to a [music] few dozen souls. The pub doubles as the post office, and neighbors measure distance in hours, not [music] kilome. Farm gates carry handpainted family names instead of numbers. And the nearest doctor can [music] be half a day away. A fact nobody brings up unless a visitor asks. Most people would call that [music] remote. New Zealand keeps a family who make it look suburban. [music] In 1980, a young man named Robert Long walked away [music] from medical school and followed the wild west coast south past the last road at Hast. He stopped [music] at the mouth of Gorge River, two full days walk from the nearest tarmac. He he moved [music] into a tiny hut between the rainforest and the Tasman Sea and simply stayed. Locals nicknamed him Bean [music] Sprout. The nickname stuck. So did he. [music] A decade later, an adventurous sailor with a master's degree, Katherine [music] Stewart, walked in and made it a family. Their two children, Kristen and Robin, grew up at Gorge River, schooled at the kitchen table, raised on the fish they caught and the garden they grew with a small plane dropping supplies roughly once a month. They have been called the most isolated family [music] in New Zealand, a title nobody has seriously challenged. [music] Ask Robert why and the answers in his [music] books circle the same quiet points. The river, the birds, [music] the time, the freedom of needing very little. It would be easy to file the longs away as hermits. But the honest word is neighbors, just very spread [music] out. In the last land on Earth that people found, somebody [music] still chooses every single day to live the way the first arrivals did, at the edge of everything and entirely at home. [music] In 1998, a location scouts [music] aircraft circled low over the green hills of Wicato, hunting for a very particular landscape on behalf of the director, Peter Jackson. Below lay the Alexander family's sheep [music] and beef farm, a rolling sea of hobbitsized hills with one perfect tree by a small lake. The family, as the story goes, was watching the rugby when the knock came. They said yes. The farm became the Shire. The Lord of the Rings films did not just borrow New Zealand's scenery. They introduced it to the planet. Fjords, volcanoes, and golden plains stood in for Middle Earth so convincingly that the country earned a nickname in the industry. The other Hollywood. A generation of travelers grew up unable to see a New Zealand mountain without hearing horns in the distance. At Hobbiton, the set was rebuilt to last, and now dozens of round painted doors sit tucked into the hillsides, smoke curling from crooked chimneys, washing strung [music] between gardens. Visitors from every country on Earth, raise a mug at the Green Dragon Inn. And just over the fence, in the same green hills, the Alexander's sheep go on grazing exactly as before. extras who never left the set on a farm that still works for a living. The country's other famous transformation [music] was not chosen. In 2011, an earthquake [music] struck Christ Church and took the heart of the city and its people with it. What happened next says everything about this place. The city refused to simply mourn. A cathedral of cardboard tubes rose as a temporary church and became beloved. Blank walls of broken [music] buildings turned into canvases for some of the boldest street [music] art in the hemisphere. Slowly, block by block, a 19th century English [music] garden city rebuilt itself into something newer and braver. Sheep [music] farms into film sets, ruins into galleries, disasters into fresh starts. This country reimagines itself the way other countries repaint a fence, which leaves only one question and one last island at the [music] very bottom of the map, where the answer is easiest to see. [music] South of the South Island, [music] across a straight with a temper, lies the country's final full stop, Stewart Island, [music] or Rakura, the land of glowing skies. A few hundred people live here, [music] most of them in the one village around the one bay with the ferry as their road [music] and the weather as their calendar. Beyond the last fence, native forest runs unbroken to cliffs that face nothing but ocean until Antarctica. [music] The island keeps New Zealand's oldest balance of power. By most counts, [music] the kiwi here outnumber the humans many times over. Almost nowhere else does the national bird [music] still wander beaches in daylight, poking the kelp for sand hoppers while people fish a polite distance away. The name Rakiora is [music] earned, too. On clear winter nights, the Aurora Australas, the southern lights, climbs the sky in silent green and rose, and the whole island steps [music] outside to watch. Life [music] at the last stop is small on paper. One school, a handful of roads, fish, tourism, and the boat schedule. But ask the people of the island or of Gorge River or the Catelins or any thin spread [music] corner of this country why they stay and the answers rhyme. Nobody locks the door. Children roam like the wcker. The sea is the pantry, the forest is the neighbor, and the sky most nights is the best television in the hemisphere. Foreigners sometimes call this country the end of the world and New Zealanders have learned to smile and agree. But stand on Rakayura at dusk with the lights of the one village coming on and the southern sky warming up its colors and the phrase quietly reverses itself. This does [music] not feel like where the world runs out. It feels like where it was left as intended. Humanity spent tens of thousands of years spreading across every land on Earth, and it found this one last. Its people seem to have decided somewhere along the way that what was found last should be kept whole. The birds still flightless, the beaches still bare, the welcome still sealed with a shared [music] breath, and the night sky still dark enough to navigate by. The way [music] the first canoes came, other countries inherited their land, New Zealanders were handed the world's final [music] blank page and chose mostly to leave it beautiful.
